sentences.translation: #Aesthetics of Japan: Awabi and Sabi
The term "sabito" is quoted without criticism today, from tourist pamphlets to philosophical papers, but there are surprisingly few attempts to revisit the concept.
This paper examines the structure of Japanese sensibility by cuddling four aesthetic concepts: apology, loneliness, ma (a room between the two) and pity.
What is apologetic?
SEN no Rikyu tried to embody the tea ceremony with a quiet beauty that resided in incompleteness, inequality and incompleteness.

The spirit of having a simple chawan with traces of hand left behind than polished gold and silver as the ultimate in beauty is fundamentally incompatible with the aesthetics of the modern West, in contrast to the values of respecting the void and the succinctness rather than the perfection.
The loneliness is different even though it is continuous.
The reason why the old mountain gates polished over the years are more beautiful than the new gates is because time itself participates in the form.
The stones, the faded axes, and the pillars with the swab—these are read as raw deposits, not as evidence of deterioration.
In other words, beauty is not to be inhabited at the time of completion, but rather to be deepened over time.
The concept of interpolation instructs different aesthetic dimensions.

The term, which describes space, silence, and void, functions as an element of expression equivalent to the filled space, whether it is architectural design, Noh interplay, or silent use in conversation.
Insufficientness is a language—this paradox is what makes the concept of interference distinct from Western emptiness and lack of.
The pity of things is a sensual concept that has been developed into court literature in the Heian period and systematically languaged by Norinaga MOTOORI.
The tightening of the chest felt when cherry blossoms were scattered is not just a sentimental wound, but a sensitive resonance of the finiteness of existence itself.

This feeling, which arises in the bond with the dwindlingly disappearing things, forms a third emotional attitude that is difficult to say pessimism or optimism, and this has created a bass sound of the Japanese literature.
Neither of these concepts resist translation because there is no corresponding foreign language vocabulary.
They are not decorative labels, but the trained style of perception itself.

Apology and pity are concepts of the world that are only open to those who have raised their eyes to see it in advance, and their acquisition is possible not by learning the meaning of the word, but by accumulation of repetitive aesthetic experiences.
The aesthetic sense of Japan is also a philosophical act to reconsider the way of feeling itself.
